title: Earth’s Gravity Redirects Juice Toward Jupiter
summary:
A planet can help a spacecraft change its speed and direction without requiring a large fuel burn. On September 28, the European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, known as Juice, used Earth’s gravity to reshape its route toward Jupiter.

The maneuver, called a gravity assist, changed Juice’s direction by 20 degrees relative to its previous path and increased its speed by 3.5 kilometers per second. Getting that result required a precisely planned approach. During the four weeks before the flyby, controllers used only one of six available opportunities to make a small course correction.

Juice reached its closest point at 11:45 UTC, passing 8,640 kilometers above the Indian Ocean. Its monitoring cameras captured a sequence of images during the encounter. Mission controllers began particularly close tracking on August 17 and planned to continue through October 10.

Spacecraft Operations Manager Angela Dietz said the careful navigation used only a small amount of the fuel reserved for the flyby. The saved fuel can support later observations of Jupiter’s icy moons.

Changing course was the main purpose of the encounter, but Earth also provided a familiar planetary target for testing scientific equipment. Teams spent months coordinating activities for Juice’s 10 instruments. Calibration means checking and adjusting an instrument so that its measurements can be interpreted reliably.

These opportunities are limited during the long journey. Earlier chances included the 2024 lunar-Earth gravity assist and observations of Comet 3I/ATLAS in 2025. For this encounter, scientists prioritized checks that would best prepare the instruments for Jupiter, while considering whether particular activities could happen later.

Power also shaped the schedule. When Juice entered Earth’s shadow, it relied on its batteries alone, affecting which activities could take place. The visit gave researchers a chance to learn how the instruments behave in space and refine tools for analyzing their data.

Juice also spent several days traveling through Earth’s magnetotail, the long extension of our planet’s magnetic field pointing away from the Sun.

The spacecraft is scheduled to make 35 flybys of Ganymede, Callisto and Europa. Those encounters will demand more complicated scientific planning than the Earth visit. Discussions about instrument operations for Europa began about 10 years ago and will continue until the planned passes in the early 2030s. This Earth encounter therefore served as both a fuel-saving maneuver and an important rehearsal.
why_it_matters: The flyby conserved fuel for observations at Jupiter and provided a rehearsal for instrument operations during the planned encounters with its icy moons.
